articleBlocks: Fed and Land hint that grass might belong in front, but they do not rule out a countryside topic yet. The opening clues stay ambiguous until Hopper gives the board a cleaner test, so this guide starts with the misleading first read, then uses the later clues to show why the final connection is narrower than the early guesses and how each clue checks that same pattern without relying on the answer reveal too early.
Stain and Roots keep the same opener alive while still feeling like a mixed list of outdoor words.
Hopper is the clue that seals it.
Grasshopper is such a specific compound that grass stops feeling thematic and starts feeling required.
Once that lands, grass-fed, grassland, grass stain, and grassroots all confirm the same pattern.
The answer was Words that come after "grass".
This board works because it mixes single-word compounds and spaced phrases without losing the same opener.
solutionNarrative: Fed and Land made a shared opener feel possible, but I could still explain the board away as something about fields or rural life. Roots helped, yet it was still possible to read the clues as thematic instead of structural.
Hopper changed that. Grasshopper is too exact to ignore, and once that compound clicked, the rest of the board immediately reorganized into grass phrases.

lessons.title: One tight compound can settle a phrase board
lessons.body: When several clues are suggestive but not conclusive, the most fixed compound often does the final confirming work.

lessons.title: Phrase boards often mix open and closed forms

lessons.title: A theme can be a trap
lessons.body: The clues can feel agricultural or outdoorsy, but the board is really about word formation, not a subject area.
